def: The study of the relationships between air, land, life, and water on Earth — the four connected spheres.
All the air and gases around Earth, including weather, wind, clouds, climate, and the jet stream.
All of Earth's water in every form — oceans, rivers, glaciers, sea ice, snow, soil moisture, aquifers, and water vapor.
All living things — plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, algae, coral reefs.
The solid Earth — rock, soil minerals, volcanoes, plate tectonics, earthquakes, fossils, magnetism.
Energy enters and leaves Earth, but very little matter does — so matter must be recycled.
An event in one sphere that causes change in another (lightning in the atmosphere ignites the biosphere).
A close, long-term relationship between two different species (mutualism, commensalism, parasitism).
Both species benefit — bees & flowers; lichen (fungus + alga).
One species benefits; the other is neither helped nor harmed — barnacles on a whale.
The parasite benefits by living on or in a host and harming it, usually without killing it quickly — tick on a deer.
A predator hunts, kills, and eats its prey — puma & mule deer.
Repeating rise and fall of predator and prey numbers; predator peaks come after prey peaks.
Organisms need the same limited resource (food, water, space, light, mates).
Competition within the SAME species — gulls competing for nesting space on a rock.
Competition between DIFFERENT species — a lion and a tiger competing for a water buffalo.
A species with a much bigger effect than its numbers suggest; removing it destroys the ecosystem's balance (wolves in Atlas NP; bees).
A change at the top of a food web that ripples down through several levels (wolves ↓ → deer ↑ → grass ↓).
An organism's feeding position in a food chain; producers are level 1.
Makes its own food from sunlight by photosynthesis — redwood sorrel. Auto = self, troph = food.
Gets energy by eating other organisms. Hetero = other.
Eats producers (an herbivore) — mule deer, brush rabbit.
Eats primary consumers — gray fox, bobcat, coyote.
Eats secondary consumers — a puma eating a gray fox.
Eats only plants / only animals / both. Omnivores (black bear) can be at more than one trophic level.
One path of energy through an ecosystem; arrows point from the food to the eater.
Many connected food chains — the most complete model of who eats whom.
Fungi and bacteria that use enzymes to break down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil for producers.
An animal that eats dead animals — vultures.
Survives on dead and decaying matter — earthworms, millipedes, banana slugs.
All the chemical reactions that keep an organism alive; it uses energy and releases some as heat.
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next; ~90% is used for metabolism and lost as heat.
A model showing the energy at each trophic level: 100% → 10% → 1% → 0.1%.
An environmental factor that slows or stops a population's growth — food, space, weather.
Has a stronger effect when the population is crowded — disease, competition, predation, waste.
Affects a population the same way at any density — floods, cold fronts, hurricanes, fire. It can still kill many!
The largest population an area can support over time with its resources (food, water, space).
J-shaped growth that gets faster and faster when resources seem unlimited.
S-shaped growth that slows and levels off at the carrying capacity.
When a population grows above its carrying capacity.
The sharp drop after an overshoot, as resources run out.
The population rises again after a decline and stabilizes around K.
A repeating rise-and-fall pattern — a population fluctuating around K, or predator–prey cycles.
Breaking a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches (roads, development, fire).
Edge = the boundary zone of a patch (more light, wind, predators); interior = deep, protected habitat.
A strip of habitat or a crossing that reconnects patches — the Highway 17 Laurel Curve undercrossing.
The gradual, fairly predictable change in the species living in an area over time.
Starts where there is NO soil — bare rock, lava, glacier-scraped granite (Yosemite).
Recovery after a disturbance that leaves the SOIL — fire, flood, abandoned farm. Faster than primary.
Soil is not intact, so humans intervene to restore the ecosystem (replanting, adding soil, erosion control).
Seeds stored in the soil that sprout after a disturbance.
The first organisms to colonize an area — lichens & mosses on rock; grasses & wildflowers after a fire.
The final, mature, relatively stable community — old-growth redwood forest.
An event that disrupts a community — natural (fire, flood, hurricane) or human (logging, clearing).
Burns along the forest floor (needles, branches, shrubs); the canopy is mostly untouched and big trees survive.
Burns through the treetops, spreading tree to tree; kills most trees (high severity).
Shrubs and low branches that carry a surface fire up into the tree crowns.
How much a fire changed or damaged the ecosystem (plants killed, soil burned): low, moderate, high.
How much heat energy a fire released — its behavior, not its effects.
A planned, low-severity surface fire set to reduce built-up fuel.
Cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers — Big Basin's climate, which dries plants into fuel.
The variety of life — ecosystems, species, and genes.
Counting organisms in sample areas to estimate the whole population or community.
The number of different species in an area.
How similar the population sizes of the species are (does one species dominate?).
Individuals of ONE species ÷ total individuals of all species (125 ÷ 200 = 0.625).
All the living things in an area (community) plus the nonliving environment, interacting.
All the members of ONE species living in an area.
All the populations (all living things) in an area — no abiotic factors.
Balance in an ecosystem; populations stay within their normal ranges over time.
An ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance; more biodiversity usually means more resilience.
A living or once-living part of an ecosystem — plants, animals, fungi, a fallen log.
A nonliving part of an ecosystem — sunlight, water, rocks, temperature, weather.
What the scientist changes on purpose (manipulated). Goes on the x-axis. Time is usually the IV.
What is measured; it responds to the IV. Goes on the y-axis.
Dependent / Responding → Y-axis; Manipulated / Independent → X-axis.
Anything kept the same so the test is fair.
Line = change over time (continuous data); bar = comparing separate categories.
Trend = the overall direction of the data; anomaly = a point that doesn't fit the pattern.
A pattern in data does not by itself prove what caused it.
One sentence that directly answers the scientific question.
Specific data — quantitative (numbers WITH units) and qualitative — that supports the claim.
A science concept that explains WHY the evidence supports the claim.
